questions.stem: In 'Hui Min ate her noodles slowly at the hawker centre.', which word is an adverb?

explain.why: 'ate' is what Hui Min did, so it is a verb
'noodles' names the food, so it is a noun
'centre' names a place, so it is a noun

solution: 'slowly' tells how Hui Min ate, so it is an adverb.

questions.stem: In 'The bus stops outside our school.', which word is a verb?

explain.why: 'outside' links 'stops' to 'our school' and shows where, so it is a preposition here
'bus' names a vehicle, so it is a noun
'school' names a place, so it is a noun

solution: 'stops' is the action the bus does, so it is the verb.

questions.stem: In 'The noisy canteen opened at seven.', which word is an adjective?

explain.why: 'at' links 'opened' to the time 'seven', so it is a preposition
'opened' is the action, so it is a verb
'canteen' names a place, so it is a noun

solution: 'noisy' describes the noun 'canteen', so it is an adjective.

questions.stem: In 'Ravi found a seat, and he sat down quietly.', which word is a pronoun?

explain.why: 'seat' names a thing, so it is a noun
'found' is an action, so it is a verb
'quietly' tells how Ravi sat, so it is an adverb

solution: 'he' stands in for 'Ravi', so it is a pronoun.

questions.stem: In 'Anna put her bag on the chair.', which word is a preposition?

explain.why: 'chair' names a thing, so it is a noun
'put' is an action, so it is a verb
'bag' names a thing, so it is a noun

solution: 'on' shows where the bag was put, so it is a preposition.

questions.stem: In 'My cousin lives in Singapore.', which word is a proper noun?

explain.why: 'in' links 'lives' to a place, so it is a preposition
'cousin' is a common noun because it is not the name of one particular person
'lives' is an action, so it is a verb

solution: 'Singapore' is the name of a particular country, so it is a proper noun.

questions.stem: In 'Mum quickly cooked dinner for us.', which word is a noun?

explain.why: 'quickly' tells how Mum cooked, so it is an adverb
'cooked' is an action, so it is a verb
'for' links 'dinner' to 'us', so it is a preposition

solution: 'dinner' names the meal that Mum cooked, so it is a noun.

questions.stem: In 'Grandma sleeps early on weekdays.', which word is a verb?

explain.why: 'Grandma' names a person, so it is a noun
'early' tells when Grandma sleeps, so it is an adverb here
'weekdays' names days, so it is a noun

solution: 'sleeps' is what Grandma does, so it is the verb.

questions.stem: In 'Ben carried a heavy bag up the stairs.', which word is an adjective?

explain.why: 'carried' is an action, so it is a verb
'stairs' names a thing, so it is a noun
'up' links 'carried' to 'the stairs', so it is a preposition

solution: 'heavy' describes the noun 'bag', so it is an adjective.

questions.stem: In 'The baby slept soundly.', which word is an adverb?

explain.why: 'baby' names a person, so it is a noun
'The' points to the noun 'baby'; it is not a word that tells how the baby slept
'slept' is an action, so it is a verb

solution: 'soundly' tells how the baby slept, so it is an adverb.

questions.stem: In 'We will visit the zoo tomorrow.', which word is an adverb?

explain.why: 'zoo' names a place, so it is a noun
'will' helps the verb 'visit' show the future; it is a helping verb
'visit' is an action, so it is a verb

solution: 'tomorrow' tells when we will visit, so it is an adverb here.

questions.stem: In 'Please give the book to me.', which word is a pronoun?

explain.why: 'book' names a thing, so it is a noun
'give' is an action, so it is a verb
'to' links 'give' to 'me', so it is a preposition

solution: 'me' stands in for the speaker, so it is a pronoun.

questions.stem: In 'The ball rolled under the bench.', which word is a preposition?

explain.why: 'ball' names a thing, so it is a noun
'rolled' is an action, so it is a verb
'bench' names a thing, so it is a noun

solution: 'under' shows where the ball rolled, so it is a preposition.

questions.stem: In 'Jun Wei stayed home because he was ill.', which word is a conjunction?

explain.why: 'home' tells where Jun Wei stayed, so it is an adverb here
'he' stands in for Jun Wei, so it is a pronoun
'stayed' is what Jun Wei did, so it is a verb

solution: 'because' joins 'Jun Wei stayed home' and 'he was ill', so it is a conjunction.

questions.stem: In 'Siti kicked the ball into the net.', which word names the subject?

explain.why: 'net' comes after the preposition 'into', so it is not the subject
'kicked' is the verb, the action itself
'ball' receives the kick, so it is the object, not the subject

solution: 'Siti' does the kicking, so 'Siti' is the subject.

questions.stem: In 'The new librarian smiled at the pupils.', what is the subject?

explain.why: 'at the pupils' is a phrase that tells who was smiled at, not who smiled
'the pupils' come after the preposition 'at', so they are not the subject
'smiled' is the verb, the action itself

solution: 'The new librarian' is the one who smiled, so it is the subject.

questions.stem: In 'The girl bought a drink at the canteen.', what is the object?

explain.why: 'bought' is the verb
'The girl' does the buying, so it is the subject
'at the canteen' tells where, so it is a phrase beginning with a preposition and not the object

solution: The girl bought 'a drink', so 'a drink' is the object.

questions.stem: In 'Dad is repairing the bicycle carefully.', what is the object?

explain.why: 'is repairing' is the verb
'carefully' tells how, so it is an adverb and not the object
'Dad' does the repairing, so he is the subject

solution: Dad is repairing 'the bicycle', so 'the bicycle' is the object.

questions.stem: Which word is the plural form of the noun 'box'?

explain.why: nouns ending in -x add -es, not just -s
'-ies' is used only for nouns ending in a consonant plus -y
'box's' shows that something belongs to the box; it is not a plural

solution: There are two 'boxes' on the shelf: a noun ending in -x adds -es.

questions.stem: Which word is the plural form of the noun 'child'?

explain.why: 'children' is already plural; adding -s is wrong
this is a misspelling of 'children'
'child' has an irregular plural, so adding -s is wrong

solution: 'The children lined up' uses 'children', the irregular plural of 'child'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the past tense?
options: We will clean the classroom after school.
We cleaned the classroom after school.
We are cleaning the classroom after school.
We clean the classroom after school.

explain.why: 'will clean' is the future tense
'are cleaning' is the present continuous tense
'clean' is the present tense

solution: 'We cleaned the classroom after school.' uses 'cleaned', the past tense.

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the future tense?
options: Our class visits the museum every year.
Our class visited the museum last week.
Our class will visit the museum next week.
Our class has visited the museum before.

explain.why: 'visits' is the present tense
'visited' is the past tense
'has visited' is the present perfect tense

solution: 'Our class will visit the museum next week.' uses 'will visit', the future tense.

questions.stem: Which sentence has its verb in the present tense?
options: Mei Ling walks to school every day.
Mei Ling was walking to school.
Mei Ling will walk to school tomorrow.
Mei Ling walked to school yesterday.

explain.why: 'was walking' is the past continuous tense
'will walk' is the future tense
'walked' is the past tense

solution: 'Mei Ling walks to school every day.' uses 'walks', the present tense.

questions.stem: Which word is the comparative form of the adjective 'tall'?

explain.why: short adjectives like 'tall' add -er instead of using 'more'
'tallish' means rather tall; it does not compare two things
'tallest' is the superlative form

solution: 'My brother is taller than I am.' compares two people, so 'taller' is the comparative.

questions.stem: Which word is the superlative form of the adjective 'good'?

explain.why: 'better' is the comparative form
'good' has an irregular superlative, so adding -est is wrong
'good' has an irregular superlative, so 'most' is wrong

solution: 'Ali is the best player in the team.' compares him with all the others, so 'best' is the superlative.

questions.stem: In 'The brave firefighter rescued the kitten.', which word is an adjective?

explain.why: 'kitten' names an animal, so it is a noun
'rescued' is an action, so it is a verb
'firefighter' names a person, so it is a noun

solution: 'brave' describes the noun 'firefighter', so it is an adjective.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'home' as an adverb?
options: Ali drew a picture of his home.
Mei Ling walked home after school.
They bought a new home last year.
Her home is near the MRT station in Bishan.

explain.why: here 'home' follows 'of his' and names a place, so it is a noun
here 'home' is the thing bought, so it is a noun
here 'home' names a place, so it is a noun

solution: In 'Mei Ling walked home after school.', 'home' tells where she walked, so it is an adverb.

questions.stem: In which sentence is 'fast' an adjective?
options: Ben pedalled fast down the slope.
Ben ran fast to catch the bus.

explain.why: 'fast' tells how Ben swims, so it is an adverb
'fast' tells how Ben pedalled, so it is an adverb
'fast' tells how Ben ran, so it is an adverb

solution: In 'Ben is a fast swimmer.', 'fast' describes the noun 'swimmer', so it is an adjective.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'well' as an adverb?
options: We drew some water from the old well.
Mei sings well in the school choir.
The water in the well is deep.

explain.why: here 'well' names a thing, so it is a noun
here 'well' describes Grandma's health, so it is an adjective
here 'well' names a thing, so it is a noun

solution: In 'Mei sings well in the school choir.', 'well' tells how she sings, so it is an adverb.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'hard' as an adverb?
options: The team trained hard for the finals.
It was a hard exam for most pupils.
Sam found the Maths paper hard.
The wooden bench at the park was hard and cold.

explain.why: 'hard' describes the noun 'exam', so it is an adjective
'hard' describes the noun 'paper', so it is an adjective
'hard' describes the noun 'bench', so it is an adjective

solution: In 'The team trained hard for the finals.', 'hard' tells how they trained, so it is an adverb.

questions.stem: In 'The girl who won the race is my cousin.', what is the word 'who'?

explain.why: 'who' does not link a noun to another word to show place or time
'who' stands for a person, 'the girl', so it is not an adverb
'who' is not an action word

solution: 'who' stands for 'the girl' and joins the clause 'who won the race' to her, so it is a relative pronoun.

questions.stem: Which word is the past participle of the verb 'write' in 'Sam has ___ to his pen pal.'?

explain.why: 'writing' is the -ing form
'writes' is the present tense
'wrote' is the simple past tense and does not follow 'has'

solution: 'Sam has written to his pen pal.' needs the past participle after 'has'.

questions.stem: Which word is the past participle of the verb 'eat' in 'The children have ___ all the cake.'?

explain.why: 'eating' is the -ing form
'eat' is irregular, so adding -ed is wrong
'ate' is the simple past tense and does not follow 'have'

solution: 'The children have eaten all the cake.' needs the past participle after 'have'.

questions.stem: Which word is the simple past tense of 'swim' in 'Yesterday, Lina ___ twenty laps.'?

explain.why: 'swum' is the past participle and is used after 'have' or 'had'
'swimming' is the -ing form and cannot be used alone here
'swim' is irregular, so adding -ed is wrong

solution: 'Yesterday, Lina swam twenty laps.' needs the simple past tense.

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the present perfect tense?

explain.why: 'finished' is the simple past tense
'is finishing' is the present continuous tense
'will finish' is the future tense

solution: 'Rina has finished her homework.' uses 'has' plus the past participle, so it is the present perfect.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the past continuous tense?
options: I am reading a comic now.
I have read the comic twice.
I read a comic before the lights went out.
I was reading a comic when the lights went out.

explain.why: 'am reading' is the present continuous tense
'have read' is the present perfect tense
'read' is the simple past tense

solution: 'was reading' in 'I was reading a comic when the lights went out.' is the past continuous.

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
options: The window was broken by the ball.
Jun Wei kicked the ball across the field.

explain.why: the subject 'The ball' does the action, so it is active
the subject 'Jun Wei' does the action, so it is active
the subject 'The boys' does the action, so it is active

solution: In 'The window was broken by the ball.', the subject receives the action, so it is passive.

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the active voice?
options: Mrs Tan marked our test papers.
Our test papers were marked by Mrs Tan.

explain.why: the subject 'papers' receives the action, so it is passive
the subject 'papers' receives the action, so it is passive
the subject 'papers' receives the action, so it is passive

solution: In 'Mrs Tan marked our test papers.', the subject 'Mrs Tan' does the action, so it is active.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the passive form of 'The cook baked the cake.'?
options: The cake was baked by the cook.
The cake baked by the cook.
The cook was baked by the cake.
The cake is baked by the cook.

explain.why: this has no verb to go with 'The cake', so it is not a complete sentence
this makes the cook the one who was baked, which changes the meaning
this changes the past tense to the present tense

solution: 'The cake was baked by the cook.' keeps the past tense and the meaning.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'This bag is ___ than that one.' with the comparative form of 'heavy'?

explain.why: 'heaviest' is the superlative, but 'than' needs a comparative
adjectives ending in a consonant plus -y change the y to i before -er
'heavy' is a short adjective, so it takes -ier, not 'more'

solution: 'This bag is heavier than that one.' compares two bags.

questions.stem: Which phrase completes 'This is the ___ garden I have ever seen.' with the superlative form of 'beautiful'?

explain.why: 'more beautiful' is the comparative, used for two things
long adjectives use 'most', not -est
long adjectives use 'most', not -est

solution: 'This is the most beautiful garden I have ever seen.' compares the garden with all others.

questions.stem: In 'Her kindness touched the whole class.', what is the word 'kindness'?

explain.why: 'kindness' is not an action
the adjective is 'kind'; 'kindness' names a quality
the adverb is 'kindly'; 'kindness' is not used to tell how

solution: 'kindness' names a quality that we cannot touch, so it is an abstract noun.

questions.stem: In 'A swarm of bees flew over the playground.', which word is a collective noun?

explain.why: 'flew' is an action, so it is a verb
'playground' names a place, so it is a common noun
'bees' names the insects that make up the group, so it is a plural noun, not the name of the group

solution: 'swarm' is the name of a group of bees, so it is a collective noun.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'The books on the table ___ mine.' so that the verb agrees with the subject?

explain.why: 'is' is singular, but the subject 'books' is plural
'am' goes only with 'I'
'be' cannot stand alone as the verb here

solution: In 'The books on the table are mine.', the plural subject 'books' needs 'are'.

questions.stem: Which pronoun correctly completes 'Mr Lim gave Amy and ___ some advice.'?

explain.why: 'myself' is used only when 'I' is also the doer of the action
'I' is a subject pronoun, but here the pronoun is the object of 'gave'
'mine' shows ownership and cannot be the object here

solution: 'Mr Lim gave Amy and me some advice.' needs the object pronoun 'me'.

questions.stem: In 'That seat is mine.', what is the word 'mine'?

explain.why: 'mine' is not the name of a particular person or place
'mine' does not tell how, when or where
'mine' is not an action word here

solution: 'mine' stands in for 'my seat' and shows ownership, so it is a possessive pronoun.

questions.stem: In which sentence is 'down' a preposition?
options: The cat ran down the stairs.
Please sit down and wait here.

explain.why: 'down' is not followed by a noun, so it is an adverb
'down' is not followed by a noun, so it is an adverb
'down' is not followed by a noun, so it is an adverb

solution: In 'The cat ran down the stairs.', 'down' is followed by 'the stairs' and shows direction, so it is a preposition.

questions.stem: In which sentence is 'run' a noun?
options: Dad goes for a run every morning.
They run a stall at the fair.
I run to school with my brother every day.

explain.why: 'run' means 'manage' here, so it is a verb
'run' is the action the speaker does, so it is a verb
'run' is the action being asked for, so it is a verb

solution: In 'Dad goes for a run every morning.', 'run' follows 'a' and names an activity, so it is a noun.

questions.stem: In 'You must wear your badge in school.', what is the word 'must'?

explain.why: the main verb is 'wear'; 'must' only helps it
'must' does not link a noun to another word
'must' does not describe a noun

solution: 'must' helps the main verb 'wear' show that something is necessary, so it is a modal verb.

questions.stem: Which group of words is a phrase and not a clause?

explain.why: this has a subject, 'Ali', and a verb, 'waited', so it is a clause
this has a subject, 'pupils', and a verb, 'lined up', so it is a clause
this has a subject, 'the bell', and a verb, 'rang', so it is a clause

solution: 'after the long recess' has no subject and verb, so it is a phrase.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the past perfect tense?
options: I had finished my lunch before the bell rang.

explain.why: 'have finished' is the present perfect tense
'was finishing' is the past continuous tense
'finished' is the simple past tense

solution: 'had finished' in 'I had finished my lunch before the bell rang.' is the past perfect.

questions.stem: Which conjunction best joins the clauses in 'Ali studied hard every night, ___ he did not pass the test.'?

explain.why: 'because' gives a reason, but not passing is not the reason for studying
'if' gives a condition, which does not fit a fact that already happened
'so' shows a result, but not passing is the opposite of what we expect

solution: 'but' shows the contrast between studying hard and not passing.

questions.stem: Which conjunction best joins the clauses in 'The match was cancelled ___ it rained heavily.'?

explain.why: 'although' shows a contrast, but the rain is the reason for the cancellation
'until' shows time up to a point, which does not give a reason
'unless' gives a condition that is not met, which does not fit a past fact

solution: 'because' gives the reason why the match was cancelled.

questions.stem: In 'We will go to the park if it stops raining.', which word joins the two clauses?

explain.why: 'to' is a preposition that links 'go' to 'the park'
'stops' is the verb in the second clause
'will' is a helping verb in the first clause

solution: 'if' joins 'We will go to the park' and 'it stops raining'.

questions.stem: In which sentence is 'that' a conjunction?
options: Mum said that dinner was ready.
The book that I borrowed is overdue.

explain.why: 'that' stands in for a thing, so it is a pronoun
'that' refers back to 'the book', so it is a relative pronoun
'That' points to the noun 'bag'

solution: In 'Mum said that dinner was ready.', 'that' joins 'Mum said' to 'dinner was ready', so it is a conjunction.

questions.stem: In which sentence is 'before' a conjunction?
options: Please finish your work before the bell rings.
Please finish your work before recess.
I have never been here before.

explain.why: 'before' is followed by the noun 'recess', so it is a preposition
'before' is followed by the noun 'dinner', so it is a preposition
'before' tells when and is followed by no clause, so it is an adverb

solution: In 'Please finish your work before the bell rings.', 'before' joins two clauses, so it is a conjunction.

questions.stem: In which sentence is 'since' a preposition?
options: I have not seen him since.
Since it was late, we took a taxi.
He has been ill since he came back from camp.

explain.why: 'since' stands alone at the end, so it is an adverb
'Since' is followed by a clause and gives a reason, so it is a conjunction
'since' is followed by a clause, so it is a conjunction

solution: In 'We have lived here since 2015.', 'since' is followed by the noun '2015', so it is a preposition.

questions.stem: In 'The box of pencils was on the desk.', which word decides that the verb is 'was' and not 'were'?

explain.why: 'desk' follows the preposition 'on' and is not the subject
'was' is the verb, not the subject
'pencils' is plural, but it sits inside 'of pencils' and is not the head of the subject

solution: The subject is 'The box of pencils', and its main noun 'box' is singular, so the verb is 'was'.

questions.stem: In 'A group of boys was waiting at the gate.', which noun is the main word of the subject?

explain.why: 'gate' follows the preposition 'at' and is not part of the subject
'boys' sits inside 'of boys' and only says who is in the group
'waiting' is part of the verb, not a noun

solution: The main word of the subject 'A group of boys' is 'group'.

questions.stem: In 'Mrs Lim gave the class a surprise quiz.', which words are the thing that was given?

explain.why: 'the class' are the people who received it
'Mrs Lim' is the subject, the one who gave
'gave' is the verb

solution: Mrs Lim gave 'a surprise quiz', so that is the object that was given.

questions.stem: In 'The vase was knocked over by the puppy.', what is the grammatical subject?

explain.why: 'the puppy' is the doer, but it comes after 'by' and is not the subject
'was knocked' is the verb
'over' is a word that goes with the verb, not the subject

solution: In 'The vase was knocked over by the puppy.', 'The vase' comes before the verb and receives the action, so it is the subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the passive form of 'The caretaker locked the gate at six.'?
options: The gate was lock by the caretaker at six.
The gate was locked by the caretaker at six.
The caretaker was locked by the gate at six.
The gate is locked by the caretaker at six.

explain.why: after 'was', the verb must be the past participle 'locked'
this makes the caretaker the one who was locked, which changes the meaning
this changes the past tense to the present tense

solution: 'The gate was locked by the caretaker at six.' keeps the past tense and the meaning.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the passive form of 'The school has repaired the roof.'?
options: The roof has been repaired by the school.
The roof had been repaired by the school.
The roof was repaired by the school.
The roof is being repaired by the school.

explain.why: this changes the tense to the past perfect
this changes the present perfect tense to the simple past tense
this changes the tense to the present continuous

solution: 'The roof has been repaired by the school.' keeps the present perfect tense.

questions.stem: In 'Although it was raining, the pupils went on the field trip.', which group of words is the main clause?
options: The pupils went on the field trip
Although it was raining, the pupils

explain.why: this cuts across both clauses and leaves out the verb of the main clause
this begins with 'Although', so it is a subordinate clause that cannot stand alone
this is part of the subordinate clause, which begins with 'Although'

solution: 'the pupils went on the field trip' can stand alone, so it is the main clause.

questions.stem: In 'We stayed indoors because the haze was thick.', which group of words is the subordinate clause?

explain.why: this has no verb, so it is not a clause
this cuts across the two clauses
this can stand alone, so it is the main clause

solution: 'because the haze was thick' cannot stand alone and gives the reason, so it is the subordinate clause.

questions.stem: In 'The children waited under the shelter.', what is 'under the shelter'?

explain.why: it has no subject and verb of its own
a noun phrase does not begin with a preposition such as 'under'
the verb of the sentence is 'waited', which is not part of this group

solution: 'under the shelter' begins with the preposition 'under' and has no verb, so it is a prepositional phrase.

questions.stem: In 'The soup was extremely hot.', which word is an adverb?

explain.why: 'was' links 'soup' to 'hot', so it is a verb
'hot' describes the noun 'soup', so it is an adjective
'soup' names a thing, so it is a noun

solution: 'extremely' tells how hot the soup was, so it is an adverb.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'light' as an adjective?
options: We light the candles at dusk.
Mum bought a light jacket for the trip.
A light flashed in the distance.

explain.why: here 'light' names a thing, so it is a noun
here 'light' is an action, so it is a verb
here 'light' names the thing that flashed, so it is a noun

solution: In 'Mum bought a light jacket for the trip.', 'light' describes the noun 'jacket', so it is an adjective.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'early' as an adjective?
options: We arrived early at the airport.
We took the early train to school.

explain.why: 'early' tells when Dad left, so it is an adverb
'early' tells when we arrived, so it is an adverb
'early' tells when Mum woke up, so it is an adverb

solution: In 'We took the early train to school.', 'early' describes the noun 'train', so it is an adjective.

questions.stem: In which sentence is 'past' a preposition?
options: In the past, our school was smaller.

explain.why: 'past' is not followed by a noun, so it is an adverb
'past' describes the noun 'week', so it is an adjective
'past' names a time, so it is a noun

solution: In 'We walked past the library.', 'past' is followed by 'the library' and shows movement, so it is a preposition.

questions.stem: Which group of words is the verb in 'The pupils were singing a song.'?

explain.why: 'a song' is the object, not part of the verb
'singing' needs 'were' before it to show the tense
'were' is only the helping verb

solution: The verb in 'The pupils were singing a song.' is 'were singing', in the past continuous tense.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'The man ___ lives next door is a pilot.' as a relative pronoun?

explain.why: 'which' is used for things, but the sentence is about a man
'whom' is used for the object, but here the pronoun is the subject of 'lives'
'whose' shows ownership, which does not fit here

solution: 'The man who lives next door is a pilot.' needs 'who' for a person as subject.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'The girl ___ bag was stolen reported it.' as a relative pronoun?

explain.why: 'which' is used for things, but the sentence is about a girl
'whom' cannot be followed by 'bag' to show ownership
'who' cannot be followed by 'bag' to show ownership

solution: 'The girl whose bag was stolen reported it.' needs 'whose' to show that the bag belongs to the girl.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the comparative form of the adjective correctly?
options: This exam was more difficult as the last one.
This exam was difficulter than the last one.
This exam was more difficult than the last one.
This exam was most difficult than the last one.

explain.why: a comparative is followed by 'than', not 'as'
long adjectives use 'more', not -er
'most' is the superlative, but 'than' needs a comparative

solution: 'more difficult than' is the correct comparative form for a long adjective.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the comparative form of the adverb correctly?
options: Ali runs more fast than Ben.

explain.why: a comparative is followed by 'than', not 'as'
'fastest' is the superlative, but 'than' needs a comparative
'fast' is short, so it takes -er, not 'more'

solution: 'Ali runs faster than Ben.' compares two people using the comparative 'faster'.

questions.stem: In 'Despite the rain, the match went on.', what is the word 'despite'?
